f: What core functions does an investment bank perform for a company raising capital?
b:
• Advises on the best way to raise long-term capital
  • Distributes the new securities to raise the money
  • Buys the issue from the company and resells it to investors (underwriting)
  • Places large blocks with the public and institutions
  • Helps the issuer comply with securities law

f: Distinguish a firm commitment underwriting from a best efforts underwriting.
b:
Firm commitment — the underwriter buys the whole issue and guarantees the company its money; unsold shares are the underwriter's loss.
Best efforts — no guarantee; the underwriter sells what it can and the company gets nothing for shares left unsold.
Tell: who eats an unsold issue?

f: Distinguish a broker from a dealer, and say what a dealer is called on an exchange vs. over the counter.
b:
Broker — an agent for the customer, paid a commission.
Dealer — a principal trading for its own account; it buys at its bid and sells at its ask.
Dealer = specialist on an exchange, market maker over the counter. Firms doing both are broker-dealers.

f: What are the defining investment traits of venture capital?
b:
Financing for privately held (often start-up) companies, typically through convertible preferred stock.
  • High risk, high potential return — some deals are total losses
  • Illiquid; low correlation with stocks
  • VC firm takes a large equity stake and helps manage
  • Goal: cash out in about 5–10 years, ideally via an IPO

f: Under Reg D Rule 501, how does an individual qualify as an accredited investor?
b:
Meet either test (2026 edition figure):
  • Net worth over $1 million, alone or with a spouse, excluding the primary residence, or
  • Income over $200,000 alone (or $300,000 joint) in each of the two most recent years, with a reasonable expectation of the same this year
Directors, executive officers and general partners of the issuer also qualify.

f: Distinguish the general partner from the limited partners in a limited partnership.
b:
General partner — runs the business, decides when distributions are paid, carries unlimited liability.
Limited partners — no role in management, limited liability; they share in income, gains, losses, deductions and credits.
Drawbacks for LPs: riskier than bonds or listed stock, usually illiquid, resale may be restricted.

f: Distinguish the primary market from the secondary market.
b:
Primary — first sale of newly issued securities; investors' money (less underwriting costs) flows to the issuing company.
Secondary — investors trade already-issued securities with one another; the issuer receives nothing.

f: Once the stop price is hit, how does a stop order differ from a stop-limit order?
b:
Both are triggered when the stock trades at or through the stop price.
Stop → becomes a market order: you get out, but a gap can fill you well below the stop.
Stop-limit → becomes a limit order: price is protected, but the trade may never execute if the stock keeps falling.

f: Where is a sell stop placed versus a buy stop, and who uses each?
b:
Sell stop — set below the current price; a long holder uses it to cut losses or protect gains in a falling market.
Buy stop — set above the current price; a short seller uses it to cap losses by buying to cover in a rising market.

f: What formula gives the stock price that triggers a margin call?
b:
Margin-call price = [purchase price × (1 − initial margin %)] ÷ (1 − maintenance margin %)
The numerator is the loan per share (debit balance per share), so it is also loan per share ÷ (1 − maintenance %).
At or below that price, equity is under the maintenance requirement and the broker demands cash.

f: Distinguish initial margin from maintenance margin.
b:
Initial margin — the share of the purchase the investor must put up: 50% under Federal Reserve Regulation T (2026 edition figure); a broker may demand more.
Maintenance margin — minimum equity % that must remain afterward; set by the broker (often 35%), with a 25% floor under NYSE Rule 431(b). Always lower than the initial margin.

f: How does the holding period return formula change when stock is bought on margin?
b:
Normal: HPR = (ending value − beginning value ± cash flows) ÷ beginning value.
On margin: same numerator, with margin interest as a negative cash flow, but divide by the investor's own initial investment (the equity put up).
Leverage magnifies the percentage gain — and the percentage loss.

f: A client is short a stock when it pays a dividend. What does the client owe, and how does it affect the return?
b:
The short seller must pay the lender of the shares a cash amount equal to the dividend.
Net profit = sale proceeds − cost to buy back − dividends paid
% return = net profit ÷ margin deposit (proceeds × initial margin %).

f: Distinguish liquidity from marketability, and name an asset that is liquid but not marketable.
b:
Liquidity — convertible to cash quickly at a known price without a meaningful loss of principal.
Marketability — can be sold quickly in an identifiable market, with no promise about price.
A money market deposit account is liquid but not marketable (only the bank redeems it); a T-bill is both.

f: Which suits a client who wants federal deposit insurance on her cash reserve: a money market deposit account (MMDA) or a money market mutual fund?
b:
The MMDA. It is a bank deposit, FDIC-insured to $250,000 per ownership category (2026 edition figure), with a minimum balance and limited checks/transfers.
A money market mutual fund is run by an open-end investment company, holds T-bills, commercial paper and negotiable CDs, and is not federally insured.

f: How is the return on a U.S. Treasury bill taxed?
b:
The bill is bought at a discount; the discount is the interest.
  • Federal: ordinary income, taxed when the bill matures
  • State and local: exempt
  • Not subject to OID rules (maturity of one year or less)
  • Sold before maturity: the gap between sale price and purchase price is taxable

f: What are the key features of commercial paper?
b:
Unsecured, negotiable short-term note issued by a large corporation to fund receivables and inventory.
  • Usually $100,000+ denominations; sold at a discount
  • Maturity of 270 days or less; rated for quality; often backed by bank credit lines
  • A bit less liquid and riskier than T-bills → slightly higher yield
  • Interest = ordinary income; money market funds are the main buyers

f: Distinguish a repurchase agreement (repo) from a reverse repo.
b:
Repo — a dealer sells government securities and agrees to buy them back later at a set, higher price. Legally a sale, in substance a collateralized loan to the dealer; the price gap is the interest (repo rate).
Reverse repo — the dealer buys the securities and later sells them back at a higher price, so the dealer is the lender.

f: A retiree says keeping most of her portfolio in CDs and money market accounts is the safe choice. What's wrong with that assumption?
b: It trades default risk for purchasing power risk: inflation steadily erodes what the interest and principal can buy. The textbook flags loss of purchasing power, not loss of principal, as one of the biggest threats to a retiree's income.

f: What is the order of the capital gain and loss netting process?
b:
1. Net short-term gains against short-term losses.
2. Net long-term gains against long-term losses.
3. If one side is a gain and the other a loss, net them to a single figure.
4. Net ST gain → ordinary rates; net LT gain → 0%/15%/20% (2026 edition figure). Net loss → deduct up to $3,000 a year and carry the rest forward indefinitely.

f: After netting, Rhea has a $7,500 net capital loss and no other capital transactions. How much can she deduct this year, and what happens to the rest?
b: She deducts $3,000 this year (2026 edition figure) and carries the remaining $4,500 forward; unused capital losses carry forward indefinitely.

f: What triggers the wash sale rule, and what happens to the disallowed loss?
b:
A sale of stock or securities at a loss when similar securities are acquired within 30 days before or after the sale (2026 edition figure).
The loss is not recognized now; it is added to the basis of the replacement shares:
New basis = cost of replacement shares + disallowed loss.

f: What holding period must a stock meet for its dividend to get the preferential qualified-dividend rates?
b: It must be held more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date (2026 edition figure). Fall short and the preferential 0%/15%/20% rates don't apply.

f: Why don't REIT and S corporation dividends get the preferential qualified-dividend rates?
b: Qualified dividends come from C corporations, whose income is taxed at the corporate level before it is paid out. REITs and S corporations are not taxed at the entity level before distributing, so their dividends don't get the preferential capital-gain rates.

f: How is the net investment income tax (NIIT) calculated?
b:
NIIT = 3.8% × the lesser of:
  • net investment income, or
  • MAGI above the threshold — $250,000 MFJ, $125,000 MFS, $200,000 all others
(2026 edition figure; textbook example thresholds.) Net investment income is investment income less certain deductible investment expenses, such as investment interest expense and early-withdrawal penalties on savings.

f: How is interest from Treasuries, corporate bonds and municipal bonds taxed at the federal and state level?
b:
Treasuries — federal yes, state no.
Corporate bonds — federal yes, state yes.
Municipal bonds — federal no (limited exceptions); state yes unless issued in the investor's home state, which can make in-state munis double tax-exempt.
